people.name: Stilicho
people.summary: Son of a Vandal officer and a Roman mother, husband of Theodosius I's niece Serena, and effective ruler of the West from 395 to 408. He fought Alaric at Pholoe, Pollentia and Verona, crushed Gildo and Radagaisus, and was destroyed by a court coup.
people.detail: His aim of controlling both courts and using Alaric to win eastern Illyricum shaped western policy and drained the Rhine and British garrisons. Claudian's poems are his propaganda; Orosius and Rutilius vilify him as a traitor who let barbarians in. His refusal to let his own troops fight to save him in 408 led to his execution and the defection of thousands of federates to Alaric.

people.name: Rufinus
people.summary: Gallic-born minister who dominated Arcadius's early reign and resisted Stilicho's claims over the East. Claudian's In Rufinum makes him a demon of greed. He was hacked to death at a military parade by Gainas's soldiers.

people.name: Eutropius
people.summary: Former slave and eunuch chamberlain who arranged Arcadius's marriage to Eudoxia, ruled the East from 395 to 399, campaigned against the Huns in Armenia and became the first eunuch consul. Brought down by Tribigild's revolt and Gainas, he was executed.

people.name: Gainas
people.summary: Gothic general in eastern service who murdered Rufinus (395), forced Eutropius's fall (399) and dominated Constantinople in 400 until the massacre of his troops. Defeated on the Hellespont, he fled north and was killed by the Hun Uldin.
people.death: killed by the Huns of Uldin, December 400

people.name: Aetius
people.summary: The dominant figure of the West from 433 to 454: hostage as a youth among Alaric's Goths and the Huns, then master of Valentinian III's government. He used Hunnic auxiliaries to crush Burgundians and Goths, and in 451 united Romans and Goths against Attila at the Catalaunian Plains.
people.detail: Procopius calls him and Bonifatius 'the last of the Romans'. His career shows the late western state's dependence on a generalissimo with personal barbarian connections. He failed to stop the loss of Africa and largely ignored Britain. Valentinian murdered him personally in 454.
people.death: killed by Valentinian III in the palace at Rome, 21/22 September 454

sources.a: Renatus Profuturus Frigeridus (in Gregory of Tours)

people.name: Bonifatius
people.summary: Heroic defender of Marseille against Athaulf (413) and correspondent of Augustine, later comes Africae. He rebelled against Placidia in 427, failed to stop the Vandals, held Hippo in 430-431, and defeated Aetius at Rimini in 432 but died of his wounds.
scholarship: Wijnendaele, The Last of the Romans: Bonifatius (2015)

people.name: Aspar
people.summary: Alan Arian general, son of Ardabur, who installed Valentinian III in 425, fought the Vandals in Africa, and as kingmaker chose Marcian (450) and Leo I (457). Leo had him murdered in 471.

people.name: Ricimer
people.summary: Grandson of the Visigothic king Wallia through his mother and of Suevic royal blood through his father, Ricimer dominated Italy for sixteen years, making and unmaking the emperors Avitus, Majorian, Libius Severus, Anthemius and Olybrius. As an Arian barbarian he could not take the throne himself.

people.name: Orestes
people.summary: Roman from Pannonia who served Attila as secretary and envoy (he appears in Priscus), later Julius Nepos's commander. He drove Nepos out in 475 and made his son Romulus emperor, then refused the federates' demand for land and was killed by Odoacer.

people.name: Marcellinus
people.summary: Friend of Aetius who after 454 made Dalmatia an autonomous command, refused to recognise Libius Severus, fought the Vandals in Sicily and Sardinia, and joined Anthemius's 468 expedition. A pagan admired for his learning, he was murdered in Sicily, probably at Ricimer's instigation. Uncle of Julius Nepos.

people.name: Aegidius
people.summary: Gallo-Roman general and loyal officer of Majorian, who after Majorian's murder refused to recognise Ricimer's emperors and governed northern Gaul independently, defeating the Visigoths at Orléans in 463. Gregory of Tours says the Franks made him their king for eight years while Childeric was in exile.

people.name: Syagrius
people.summary: Son of Aegidius, ruler of the Roman enclave around Soissons, called 'king of the Romans' by Gregory of Tours. Defeated by Clovis in 486, he fled to the Visigoths, who surrendered him to be executed.

people.name: Illus
people.summary: Isaurian general whose defection restored Zeno in 476 and who dominated his government until 484, when he rebelled and crowned Leontius. A patron of intellectuals, he held out in the fortress of Papyrius until 488.
people.death: beheaded after the fall of Papyrius, 488

people.name: Vitalian
people.summary: Thracian commander who led three rebellions (513-515) against Anastasius in the name of Chalcedonian orthodoxy and federate pay. Rehabilitated by Justin I, he was consul in 520 and murdered that year, probably at Justinian's instigation.

people.name: Belisarius
people.summary: Justinian's greatest general, born in Germania on the Thracian-Illyrian border. He won at Dara (530), lost at Callinicum (531), suppressed the Nika riots (532), destroyed the Vandal kingdom (533-534), took Sicily, Naples, Rome and Ravenna (535-540), fought Persia (541-542) and returned to Italy (544-549) with inadequate resources. In 559 he saved Constantinople from the Kutrigurs.
people.detail: Procopius, his secretary, wrote the Wars largely around him and the Secret History partly against him, depicting him as dominated by his wife Antonina. He was twice disgraced (542 and 562) and restored. The medieval legend of the blinded beggar Belisarius asking for an obol is a later fiction popularised by Marmontel's novel and David's painting.
scholarship: Hughes, Belisarius: The Last Roman General (2009)

people.name: Narses
people.summary: Persarmenian eunuch and chamberlain who bribed the Blues during the Nika riots, served in Italy alongside Belisarius in 538-539, and in 551-554, in his seventies, finished the Gothic War with victories at Busta Gallorum and Mons Lactarius and destroyed the Frankish-Alamannic invasion at the Volturnus. He governed Italy until 568.
people.detail: Paul the Deacon reports the tale that Sophia insulted him, telling him to come and spin wool with the women, and that in revenge he invited the Lombards; historians reject this. He was celebrated for piety toward the Virgin, who reportedly told him when to fight.

people.name: John the Cappadocian
people.summary: Justinian's ruthless finance minister, who abolished much of the public post, centralised tax collection and squeezed provincials and the wealthy. Dismissed at the crowd's demand during Nika and reinstated, he was brought down in 541 by a sting organised by Theodora and Antonina, ordained a priest by force and exiled.

people.name: Tribonian
people.summary: Pamphylian lawyer who directed the compilation of the Digest, edited the Institutes and the second Codex, and drafted many Novels. Procopius accuses him of selling justice and of paganism; he was dismissed during Nika and restored.

people.name: Germanus
people.summary: Justinian's cousin, who defeated the Antae in Thrace, won back the mutinous army of Africa and defeated Stotzas (537), and in 550 married Matasuntha, Theodoric's granddaughter, as he prepared to lead the final Italian campaign. He died before setting out; Jordanes celebrates his son as a union of Amal and Anician blood.

people.name: John Troglita
people.summary: Veteran of Belisarius's African and eastern campaigns, sent to Africa in 546. After a defeat at Marta in 547, he crushed the Moorish confederation at the Campi Catonis in 548. He is the hero of Corippus's eight-book Latin epic, the Iohannis.

people.name: Solomon

roles.t: Praetorian prefect and magister militum of Africa
Praetorian prefect and magister militum of Africa

people.summary: Eunuch officer from Dara who governed Roman Africa twice, fought the Moors of the Aurès mountains and built the network of fortifications whose ruins survive across Tunisia and Algeria. Killed fighting the Moors at Cillium.

people.name: Priscus
people.summary: Maurice's most successful Balkan commander, who campaigned beyond the Danube against the Slavs (593) and won the victories of 599 deep in Avar territory. Under Phocas he married Phocas's daughter and commanded the excubitors, then helped Heraclius take power, but was forced into a monastery in 612.
people.death: died as a monk at Constantinople, 613

people.name: Philippicus
people.summary: Maurice's brother-in-law, victor at Solachon (586) where he paraded the Camuliana icon; sometimes proposed as the author of the Strategikon. He became a monk under Phocas and served Heraclius as a general in 611-613.
people.death: died as a monk at Chrysopolis, c. 614

people.name: Comentiolus
people.summary: Maurice's loyal but much criticised general, active in the Balkans, the East and Spain (an inscription at Cartagena records his fortification of the city). Theophylact blames him for the disastrous retreat of 598-599 that led to the massacre of 12,000 captives. Phocas executed him.

people.name: Shahrbaraz
people.summary: Khosrow II's greatest general ('Boar of the Empire'), conqueror of Jerusalem (614) and Egypt (619), who camped at Chalcedon during the siege of 626. Alienated from Khosrow, he negotiated with Heraclius, returned the True Cross and evacuated Roman lands, then seized the Sasanian throne in 630.
people.death: murdered after a reign of about 40 days, June 630

people.name: Shahin
people.summary: Persian general who campaigned in Armenia and Anatolia, reached Chalcedon in 615, and fought alongside Shahrbaraz at Antioch (613). Defeated by Heraclius's brother Theodore in 626, he is said to have died of grief, after which Khosrow abused his corpse.

people.name: Theodore (brother of Heraclius)
people.summary: Heraclius's brother and chief lieutenant, who fought at Antioch (613), defeated Shahin (626), and commanded against the Arabs in Syria in 634-636, probably losing at Ajnadayn. Disgraced after quarrelling with Martina, he was sent to Constantinople in chains.

people.name: Vahan
people.summary: Armenian commander of the Roman army at the Yarmuk (636). Theophanes says his troops proclaimed him emperor before the battle. His fate after the defeat is unknown; Arab tradition says he died or became a monk at Sinai.

people.name: Alaric I
people.summary: Gothic leader who forged the people later called Visigoths out of Theodosius's federates, ravaged Greece (395-397), invaded Italy twice, and in 410 sacked Rome. His aims were consistent and Roman: a regular command, pay, grain and land for his people.
people.detail: He played the eastern and western courts against each other for fifteen years. After Stilicho's death his army swelled with defecting federates and fugitive slaves. He died seeking passage to Africa and was buried in the bed of the Busento, according to Jordanes.
scholarship: Burns, Barbarians within the Gates of Rome (1994)

people.name: Athaulf
people.summary: Brother-in-law and successor of Alaric, who led the Goths from Italy to Gaul (412), married Galla Placidia at Narbonne (414), and moved to Barcelona, where he was murdered by a retainer. Orosius credits him with wishing to restore the Roman name with Gothic strength.

people.name: Wallia
people.summary: Gothic king who made peace with Constantius in 416, returned Galla Placidia for grain, destroyed the Siling Vandals and Alans in Spain as Roman federates, and received the settlement in Aquitaine in 418. Grandfather of Ricimer.

people.name: Theodoric I
people.summary: King of the Visigoths at Toulouse for 33 years, who tried repeatedly to expand toward Arles and Narbonne, defeated Litorius in 439, and died leading his people against Attila at the Catalaunian Plains.

people.name: Euric
people.summary: Murdered his brother Theodoric II in 466 and broke with Rome, conquering Gaul south of the Loire and west of the Rhône (with Provence by 476) and most of Spain. His Code (Codex Euricianus, c. 475) is the earliest surviving Germanic law code, written in Latin by Roman jurists.

people.name: Alaric II
people.summary: Son of Euric, who issued the Breviary of Alaric (506) and convened the Council of Agde (506) to win his Catholic Roman subjects. Married to Theodoric the Great's daughter Thiudigotho, he was killed by Clovis at Vouillé.

people.name: Radagaisus
people.summary: Pagan Gothic king who invaded Italy from the middle Danube in 405 with a large following, probably displaced by the Huns. Trapped by Stilicho at Faesulae, he was executed; 12,000 of his men were drafted into the Roman army.

people.name: Gaiseric

roles.t: King of the Vandals and Alans

people.summary: The most formidable barbarian king of the fifth century: he led the Vandals and Alans to Africa (429), took Carthage (439), built the only barbarian navy, sacked Rome (455) and destroyed Majorian's (460) and Leo's (468) expeditions, before making perpetual peace with Zeno (474).
people.detail: Jordanes describes him as of medium height, lame from a fall from a horse, a man of few words who despised luxury. He persecuted the Nicene church, confiscated senatorial estates, and married his son Huneric to Valentinian III's daughter Eudocia. His dating of his reign from the fall of Carthage signals a claim to sovereignty no other federate king made so early.

people.name: Huneric

roles.t: King of the Vandals and Alans

people.summary: Son of Gaiseric, hostage in Italy after 435 and husband of Eudocia, daughter of Valentinian III. His reign culminated in the persecution of Nicene Christians in 484 described by Victor of Vita.

people.name: Gelimer

roles.t: King of the Vandals and Alans

people.summary: Last Vandal king, who deposed his pro-Roman cousin Hilderic in 530, providing Justinian's pretext for war. Defeated at Ad Decimum and Tricamarum, he surrendered on Mount Papua and walked in Belisarius's triumph, then retired to estates in Galatia.

people.name: Attila
people.summary: Ruler of a Hunnic empire stretching from the Alps to the Black Sea steppe, who extracted vast tribute from Constantinople, devastated the Balkans (441-447), invaded Gaul (451) and Italy (452), and died on his wedding night in 453. His empire collapsed within a year.
people.detail: Priscus, who saw him in 449, describes a short, broad man with small eyes and a flat nose, frugal amid luxury. His power rested on extracting Roman gold and redistributing it to a multiethnic elite (Goths, Gepids, Romans like Orestes and Onegesius). Modern scholarship (Kelly, Kim, Maenchen-Helfen) stresses the sophistication of this system, while Heather sees the Hunnic empire as the indirect cause of western collapse.
people.death: haemorrhage on his wedding night, early 453
scholarship: Maenchen-Helfen, The World of the Huns (1973)

people.name: Bleda
people.summary: Attila's elder brother and co-ruler, who negotiated the Treaty of Margus and shared the Balkan campaigns of 441-442. Priscus tells of his fondness for the Moorish dwarf Zercon, whom he dressed in a comic suit of armour. Attila had him killed.

people.name: Rua
people.summary: Uncle of Attila and Bleda, the first Hunnic king to receive a regular annual tribute (350 lbs of gold) from Constantinople; he supported Aetius in 425 and 433. He died, struck by lightning according to Socrates, while threatening Thrace.

people.name: Theodoric the Great
people.summary: Amal Gothic king, raised as a hostage in Constantinople from age eight, who after years of Balkan warfare invaded Italy for Zeno in 488, killed Odoacer (493), and ruled Italy for 33 years, also regent of the Visigothic kingdom from 511. His reign preserved Roman administration, Senate and culture under Gothic military rule.
people.detail: He married Clovis's sister and allied his daughters and nieces with the Visigothic, Burgundian, Vandal and Thuringian royal houses, creating a western network of kingdoms. His building programme in Ravenna (Sant'Apollinare Nuovo, the Arian Baptistery, his mausoleum) and restorations in Rome continued imperial patterns. His last years were darkened by the executions of Boethius and Symmachus and the imprisonment of Pope John I. Remembered as Dietrich von Bern in Germanic epic.
scholarship: Arnold, Theoderic and the Roman Imperial Restoration (2014)

people.name: Theodoric Strabo
people.summary: 'The Squinter', leader of the Gothic federates in Thrace and kinsman of Aspar's wife, rival of Theodoric the Amal for Roman favour throughout the 470s. He died when his horse threw him onto a spear rack; his followers joined the Amal.

people.name: Witiges
people.summary: Gothic soldier elected king in 536 after Theodahad's failure, who married Theodoric's granddaughter Matasuntha, besieged Rome for a year (537-538), sought Persian help against Justinian, and surrendered Ravenna to Belisarius in 540. He died a patrician in Constantinople.

people.name: Totila
people.summary: Gothic king who revived the war after 541, retook most of Italy, captured Rome twice (546 and 550), and won over Italian peasants and slaves against senatorial landowners. He was killed at Busta Gallorum. His coins bear the name Baduila.

people.name: Teia
people.summary: Last Ostrogothic king, elected at Pavia after Totila's death. He killed Roman hostages, then marched south to relieve Cumae and died fighting at Mons Lactarius; Procopius praises his courage as equal to any hero's.

people.name: Clovis I
people.summary: Merovingian king who united the Franks, defeated Syagrius (486), the Alamanni, and the Visigoths at Vouillé (507), and converted to Catholic Christianity, aligning his kingdom with the Gallo-Roman church. Recognised by Anastasius in 508, he made Paris his capital.
people.detail: Gregory of Tours's account, written seventy years later, is shaped as a Constantine-like conversion story. The dates of key events, especially his baptism, are uncertain. His son Theuderic's and grandsons' conquests completed the Frankish domination of Gaul.

people.name: Alboin
people.summary: Lombard king who destroyed the Gepids with Avar help (567) and in 568 led his people into Italy, taking the Po valley. He was murdered at Verona at the instigation of his wife Rosamund, daughter of the Gepid king whose skull he used as a cup.

people.name: Bayan I
people.summary: Avar khagan who led his people into the Carpathian basin (567-568), took Sirmium (582) and for thirty years raided and extorted the Balkans with Slav auxiliaries. Menander and Theophylact portray him as a cunning negotiator. His death date is uncertain; his sons led the Avars in the 599 campaign and the siege of 626.

people.name: Kavad I
people.summary: Sasanian king who supported the egalitarian Mazdakite movement, was deposed and escaped to the Hephthalites, and returned to power in 499. His demand for Roman subsidies led to the wars of 502-506 and 526-532 (the sieges of Amida, Dara and Callinicum).

people.name: Khosrow I
people.summary: The greatest Sasanian king in Persian memory, 'of the immortal soul'. He reformed taxation and the army, made the Eternal Peace (532), sacked Antioch (540), fought the Lazic War, made the Fifty Years' Peace (562), destroyed the Hephthalites with Turkic help, and took Dara (573).
people.detail: Greek sources (Agathias) mock his pretensions to philosophy, though he welcomed the exiled Athenian Neoplatonists in 531-532. Under him Indian texts (Panchatantra, chess) were translated into Middle Persian. His reforms built the fiscal-military machine that his grandson Khosrow II used against Rome.

people.name: Khosrow II
people.summary: 'The Victorious', restored by Maurice in 591, who after Maurice's murder waged the great war of 603-628, conquering Mesopotamia, Syria, Palestine (with the True Cross), Egypt and much of Anatolia, before Heraclius's counteroffensive led to his overthrow and execution by his own son.
people.detail: Married to the Roman Christian Maria (according to tradition) and to the Aramaean Christian Shirin, he patronised Christian shrines such as that of St Sergius at Resafa while holding Jerusalem's relics. The reliefs at Taq-e Bostan are attributed to him. His destruction of the Lakhmid buffer state (602) opened the Iraqi frontier to Arab raiders.
people.death: executed on the orders of Kavad II, February 628
scholarship: Howard-Johnston, The Last Great War of Antiquity (2021)

people.name: Bahram Chobin
people.summary: Parthian noble of the Mihran house who defeated the Turks, rebelled against Hormizd IV, and became the first non-Sasanian to take the Persian throne. Defeated by Khosrow II with Roman help at the Blarathon, he fled to the Turks and was assassinated. He became a hero of Persian romance.

people.name: Odoacer
people.summary: Officer of Scirian origin, son of Edeco (Attila's envoy in 449), who as leader of the federate army deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476 and ruled Italy as king for 17 years, keeping the Senate and Roman administration. He took Dalmatia (481) and destroyed the Rugii (487). Zeno sent Theodoric against him; Theodoric killed him at a banquet.
people.death: killed by Theodoric at Ravenna, 15 March 493

people.name: Gundobad
people.summary: Ricimer's nephew, who beheaded Anthemius in 472, made Glycerius emperor, then returned to rule the Burgundians for over forty years. He issued the Liber Constitutionum (Lex Gundobada) and a Roman law for his Roman subjects, and allied with Clovis at Vouillé.
